newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition stays together, but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: German coalition stays together, but doubts remain.

text.p: Leaders of Germany's fragile coalition pledged on Monday to stick together, but differences over raising taxes to plug a yawning deficit and qualify for Europe's single currency still cast a shadow over the government.

As reports surfaced that Chancellor Helmut Kohl had threatened to resign over the budget dilemma, leaders of his centre-right coalition said the 14-year-old alliance between the Christian Democrats and Free Democrats would survive.

Erwin Teufel, a CDU leader and state premier of Baden- Wuerttemberg, said he expected the coalition would weather the current storm, but added there was nevertheless a possibility it could collapse because of the budget dispute.
"The situation reminds me of 1966," said Teufel before a meeting of CDU leaders in Bonn, referring to the last time a coalition made up of Christian Democrats and liberals broke up.
"No one wanted the coalition to end then either, but it just happened," he said.
The Hamburger Morgenpost newspaper said on Monday that Kohl had threatened to resign on four occasions last week over the budget row. But a chancellery spokesman denied the report.

The newspaper quoted coalition sources saying that Kohl had offered to quit during two crisis meetings held in his chancellery last Sunday and Tuesday. Last November Kohl threatened to resign amid a row over the 1997 budget.

But commentators said they believed it had been an empty threat that Kohl was easily talked out of because leaders of both the CDU and FDP realise there are few palatable alternatives to remaining in the coalition.

Wolfgang Gerhardt, the FDP chairman, told journalists in Bonn on Monday the differences were narrowing between his party and Kohl's CDU on new budget savings measures without tax increases in 1997 and 1998.
"The coalition will stick together," said Gerhardt.

But the Hamburger Morgenpost newspaper reported on Monday that Waigel had met former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt to discuss the possible formation of a grand coalition between the Social Democrats (SPD) and the CDU/CSU if the coalition breaks apart.

Schmidt's office confirmed the meeting. In a separate television interview on Monday the former chancellor called on Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel to resign over what he said was the government's fiscal mismanagement.

The fierce fighting over the gaping holes for both the 1997 and 1998 budgets has torn at the threads of the coalition for months. The FDP has firmly opposed any tax increases while Waigel refuses to rule out raising some taxes in 1998.

The failure to close the budget holes has cut the chances Germany will meet fiscal requirements for European economic and monetary union. The Maastricht Treaty permits budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
The deficits and prospects Germany will not qualify for the euro opened the door to a heated debate on the euro that had long been stifled by a broad consensus among political elites.
Some leaders have now proposed taking a more relaxed view on the Maastricht criteria while others have argued to delay EMU.

But Kohl has warned of dire consequences if the euro were delayed and said on Sunday he was convinced Germany would qualify on time for the euro without softening the entry rules, a sentiment supported by the beleaguered Waigel.
"We will do everything we can in the next months to fulfill the criteria," Waigel told Bild daily on Monday.

Speaking in Luxembourg, Waigel stressed the importance of budget discipline and stable prices and said the stability pact aimed at creating a solid basis for Europe's planned single currency was not up for discussion.
"What has been agreed upon and discussed for two years can no longer be put up for negotiation," he said.
But Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, a powerful Waigel rival and critic, insisted that meeting the Maastricht criteria was more important than the timetable.
Christoph Zeitler, a member of the Bundesbank council, said relaxing the criteria was not an appropriate solution.
The chief economist of Deutsche Bank, Norbert Walter, said on Monday it was naive and destructive to talk of delaying EMU.
"Only children believe there is a realistic chance of an orderly one or two-year delay," Walter said, adding a less rigid approach to the Maastricht Treaty criteria was needed.
